## Right to Cure a Default in Hawaii [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/hawaii.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in Hawaii [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Hawaii residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Hawaii

In Hawaii, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Hawaii:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Hawaii real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Hawaii Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Hawaii offers judicial and non-judicial foreclosure (HRS Chapter 667). Mortgage Foreclosure Dispute Resolution program available.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Hawaii Retail Installment Cure

HRS Chapter 476 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Hawaii law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Hawaii UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

HRS Chapter 490 Article 9 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many Hawaii consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where Hawaii state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Cure any default on a long-term debt (typically a mortgage) within a reasonable time.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the Hawaii debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Hawaii law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Hawaii

The practical cure window in Hawaii depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Hawaii cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Hawaii practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Hawaii

If the Hawaii borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Idaho residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Idaho

In Idaho, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Idaho:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Idaho real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Idaho Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Idaho Code Section 45-1506 permits reinstatement up to 115 days after notice of default by paying arrearages.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Idaho Code Section 28-43-303 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Idaho law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Idaho UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

Idaho Code Title 28 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Idaho law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Idaho

The practical cure window in Idaho depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Idaho cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Idaho practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Source: https://righttocure.org/states/iowa.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in Iowa [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Iowa residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Iowa

In Iowa, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Iowa:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Iowa real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Iowa Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Iowa Code Chapter 654 (judicial foreclosure). Reinstatement available; mediation encouraged under 654A.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Iowa Retail Installment Cure

Iowa Code Section 537.5111 requires notice of right to cure for consumer credit.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Iowa law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Iowa UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

Iowa Code Chapter 554, Article 9 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many Iowa consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where Iowa state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Cure any default on a long-term debt (typically a mortgage) within a reasonable time.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the Iowa debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Iowa law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Iowa

The practical cure window in Iowa depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Iowa cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Iowa practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Iowa

If the Iowa borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

## Right to Cure a Default in Kansas [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

Right to Cure a Default in Kansas [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Kansas residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Kansas

In Kansas, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Kansas:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Kansas real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Kansas Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Kansas uses judicial foreclosure (K.S.A. 60-2410). Reinstatement available before sale.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Kansas Retail Installment Cure

K.S.A. 16a-5-110 (Uniform Consumer Credit Code) requires notice of right to cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Kansas law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Kansas UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

K.S.A. Chapter 84 Article 9 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many Kansas consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Kansas law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Kansas

The practical cure window in Kansas depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Kansas cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Kansas practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Kansas

If the Kansas borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

Kansas Federal Bankruptcy Data

When state-law cure fails or a creditor refuses reinstatement, bankruptcy becomes the cure mechanism. Kansas's Chapter 13 data below shows the scale where plan-based cure under Section 1322(b)(5) is used.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 40,849 consumer bankruptcy cases from Kansas's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 718,67399.4%0.5%

Chapter 1322,17673.1%26.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Kentucky real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Kentucky Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Kentucky uses judicial foreclosure (KRS 426). Reinstatement through payment of arrears before sale.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

KRS 371.220 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Where Kentucky law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Right to Cure a Default in Louisiana [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Louisiana residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Louisiana

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Louisiana:

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maine residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Maine

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Maine law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Maine practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Maine

If the Maine borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

## Right to Cure a Default in Maryland [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/maryland.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in Maryland [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maryland residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Maryland

In Maryland, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Maryland:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Maryland real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Maryland Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Maryland uses judicial foreclosure with redemption through Md. Code Real Prop. Section 7-105 et seq. Mediation program available.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Maryland Retail Installment Cure

Md. Code Com. Law Section 12-1018 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Maryland law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Maryland UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

Md. Code Com. Law Section 9-611 et seq. codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many Maryland consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where Maryland state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Cure any default on a long-term debt (typically a mortgage) within a reasonable time.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the Maryland debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Maryland law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Maryland

The practical cure window in Maryland depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Maryland cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Maryland practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Maryland

If the Maryland borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

Maryland Federal Bankruptcy Data

When state-law cure fails or a creditor refuses reinstatement, bankruptcy becomes the cure mechanism. Maryland's Chapter 13 data below shows the scale where plan-based cure under Section 1322(b)(5) is used.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 559 consumer bankruptcy cases from Maryland's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 742097.4%0.0%

Chapter 13139n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Right to Cure a Default in Mississippi [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Mississippi residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Mississippi

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Mississippi Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Mississippi uses non-judicial foreclosure (Miss. Code Section 89-1-55). No statutory reinstatement right; cure depends on deed terms.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Mississippi Retail Installment Cure

Miss. Code Section 63-19-57 governs motor vehicle retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Mississippi law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Mississippi UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

Miss. Code Title 75 Article 9 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many Mississippi consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where Mississippi state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Cure any default on a long-term debt (typically a mortgage) within a reasonable time.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the Mississippi debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Mississippi law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Mississippi

The practical cure window in Mississippi depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Mississippi cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Mississippi practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Mississippi

If the Mississippi borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

## Right to Cure a Default in Missouri [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/missouri.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in Missouri [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Missouri residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Missouri

In Missouri, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Missouri:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Missouri real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Missouri Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Missouri uses non-judicial foreclosure under deed of trust (RSMo Chapter 443). Reinstatement typically negotiable.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Missouri Retail Installment Cure

RSMo 408.554 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Missouri law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Missouri UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

RSMo Chapter 400 Article 9 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many Missouri consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where Missouri state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Cure any default on a long-term debt (typically a mortgage) within a reasonable time.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the Missouri debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Missouri law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Missouri

The practical cure window in Missouri depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Missouri cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Missouri practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Missouri

If the Missouri borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

Missouri Federal Bankruptcy Data

When state-law cure fails or a creditor refuses reinstatement, bankruptcy becomes the cure mechanism. Missouri's Chapter 13 data below shows the scale where plan-based cure under Section 1322(b)(5) is used.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 45,771 consumer bankruptcy cases from Missouri's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 722,13299.0%0.8%

Chapter 1323,63955.1%44.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

## Right to Cure a Default in New Hampshire [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/new-hampshire.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in New Hampshire [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Hampshire residents.

Right to Cure a Default in New Hampshire

In New Hampshire, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in New Hampshire:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under New Hampshire real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

New Hampshire Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

NH uses non-judicial foreclosure (RSA 479). No statutory reinstatement right; cure depends on mortgage terms.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

New Hampshire Retail Installment Cure

RSA 361-A (Retail Installment Sales Act) governs.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where New Hampshire law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

New Hampshire UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

RSA 382-A:9-611 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many New Hampshire consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where New Hampshire state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Cure any default on a long-term debt (typically a mortgage) within a reasonable time.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the New Hampshire debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under New Hampshire law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in New Hampshire

The practical cure window in New Hampshire depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

New Hampshire cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

New Hampshire practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in New Hampshire

If the New Hampshire borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

Related New Hampshire Resources

Auto loan cure

Chapter 13 bankruptcy cure

Cure timeline

Notice requirements

Reinstatement vs cure

After-cure default

## Right to Cure a Default in New Jersey [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/new-jersey.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in New Jersey [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Jersey residents.

Right to Cure a Default in New Jersey

In New Jersey, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in New Jersey:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under New Jersey real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

New Jersey Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

New Jersey uses judicial foreclosure (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-2.3 et seq.). Fair Foreclosure Act requires cure notice; reinstatement available before judgment and often up to sale.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

N.J.S.A. 17:16C-41 (Retail Installment Sales Act) governs.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where New Jersey law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

N.J.S.A. 12A:9-611 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many New Jersey consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under New Jersey law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in New Jersey

The practical cure window in New Jersey depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

New Jersey cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

New Jersey practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in New Jersey

If the New Jersey borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

New Jersey Federal Bankruptcy Data

When state-law cure fails or a creditor refuses reinstatement, bankruptcy becomes the cure mechanism. New Jersey's Chapter 13 data below shows the scale where plan-based cure under Section 1322(b)(5) is used.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,580 consumer bankruptcy cases from New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

## Right to Cure a Default in New York [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/new-york.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in New York [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New York residents.

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Carolina residents.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the North Carolina debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under North Carolina law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in North Carolina

The practical cure window in North Carolina depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

North Carolina cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

North Carolina practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in North Carolina

If the North Carolina borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

North Carolina Federal Bankruptcy Data

When state-law cure fails or a creditor refuses reinstatement, bankruptcy becomes the cure mechanism. North Carolina's Chapter 13 data below shows the scale where plan-based cure under Section 1322(b)(5) is used.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 827 consumer bankruptcy cases from North Carolina's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7273n/an/a

Chapter 13554n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

## Right to Cure a Default in North Dakota [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/north-dakota.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in North Dakota [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Dakota residents.

Right to Cure a Default in North Dakota

In North Dakota, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in North Dakota:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under North Dakota real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

North Dakota Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

ND Century Code Chapter 32-19 (judicial foreclosure). Reinstatement available under 32-19-07.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

North Dakota Retail Installment Cure

NDCC Section 51-13-02 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where North Dakota law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

North Dakota UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

NDCC Title 41 Article 9 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many North Dakota consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where North Dakota state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Cure any default on a long-term debt (typically a mortgage) within a reasonable time.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the North Dakota debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under North Dakota law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in North Dakota

The practical cure window in North Dakota depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

North Dakota cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

North Dakota practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in North Dakota

If the North Dakota borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

## Right to Cure a Default in Ohio [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/ohio.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in Ohio [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Ohio

In Ohio, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Ohio:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Ohio real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Ohio Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

Ohio Revised Code Section 1343.01 addresses interest and acceleration on notes. Ohio uses judicial foreclosure; reinstatement available before confirmation of sale.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Ohio Retail Installment Cure

ORC Chapter 1317 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Ohio law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Ohio UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

ORC Chapter 1309 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many Ohio consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where Ohio state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the Ohio debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Ohio law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Ohio

The practical cure window in Ohio depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Ohio cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Ohio practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Ohio

If the Ohio borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

Right to Cure a Default in Pennsylvania [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Pennsylvania residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Pennsylvania

In Pennsylvania, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Pennsylvania:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Pennsylvania real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Pennsylvania Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

41 P.S. Section 403 (Act 6 of 1974) requires a 30-day Act 6 notice of intent to foreclose for residential mortgages. Reinstatement available through foreclosure judgment.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Pennsylvania Retail Installment Cure

12 P.S. Section 6203 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Pennsylvania law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

Pennsylvania UCC Article 9 Default and Cure

13 Pa. C.S. Section 9611 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The secured party must send reasonable notice of disposition before selling repossessed collateral.

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.

Any post-sale deficiency calculation depends on whether the disposition was commercially reasonable.

In consumer transactions, UCC 9-625 provides statutory damages for a non-compliant disposition equal to the credit service charge plus 10% of the principal. Many Pennsylvania consumer defense strategies center on proving non-compliance with Article 9 to eliminate deficiency judgments.

See auto loan cure and repossession.

Section 1322(b)(5) Mortgage Cure in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Where Pennsylvania state-law cure fails - because the acceleration has already occurred, the sale date is too close, or the creditor will not accept a reinstatement quote - federal bankruptcy law provides a second path under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5).

Under 1322(b)(5), a Chapter 13 plan may:

Cure any default on a long-term debt (typically a mortgage) within a reasonable time.

Maintain contractual payments on the debt going forward while the arrears are cured through the plan.

Preserve the original maturity of the loan.

The 1322(c) proviso gives the Pennsylvania debtor the right to cure a mortgage default "until such residence is sold at a foreclosure sale that is conducted in accordance with applicable nonbankruptcy law." This means that, as long as the Chapter 13 petition is filed before the foreclosure sale is completed under Pennsylvania law, the plan can cure the default and reinstate the mortgage.

See bankruptcy cure overview.

Cure Timeline in Pennsylvania

The practical cure window in Pennsylvania depends on the collateral:

Mortgage: from first missed payment through foreclosure sale; state cure notice (if any) plus 1322(c) bankruptcy-cure window.

Vehicle: state retail installment notice period (typically 14-30 days) plus pre-sale UCC 9-614 notice.

Other secured: UCC Article 9 pre-disposition notice (typically 10 days of notification before sale).

Timing matters: once the state-law sale is complete, the cure right is gone. For mortgages, chapter 13 filing before the foreclosure sale is the last-ditch option.

See cure timeline.

Notice Requirements

Pennsylvania cure notices must typically:

Identify the amount required to cure (or a calculation).

State the cure period (e.g., 20 days).

State the consequences of failure to cure (acceleration, repossession, foreclosure).

Be sent in writing, usually by certified mail to the borrower's last known address.

A deficient notice is a defense. See notice requirements.

Reinstatement vs. Cure

Pennsylvania practice distinguishes reinstatement from cure:

Reinstatement - bringing the account current and restoring it to non-default status. Typical in mortgage context.

Cure - a broader statutory or contractual right to correct default, sometimes with a specific window and notice.

Redemption - paying the full balance (not arrears) to prevent sale. A fallback if reinstatement is unavailable.

See reinstatement vs cure.

After-Cure Default in Pennsylvania

If the Pennsylvania borrower cures but defaults again, creditor's treatment depends on contract and state law:

Mortgage: typically subject to new notice cycle, unless a prior court order bars subsequent cure.

Vehicle RISA: under some state statutes, the borrower has only one statutory cure per contract year.

UCC-9: no statutory limit on cure attempts, but practical leverage erodes.

See after-cure default.

Pennsylvania Federal Bankruptcy Data

When state-law cure fails or a creditor refuses reinstatement, bankruptcy becomes the cure mechanism. Pennsylvania's Chapter 13 data below shows the scale where plan-based cure under Section 1322(b)(5) is used.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,513 consumer bankruptcy cases from Pennsylvania's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7415n/an/a

Chapter 131,098n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

## Right to Cure a Default in Rhode Island [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9
Source: https://righttocure.org/states/rhode-island.html

← righttocure.org home

Right to Cure a Default in Rhode Island [2026]: Mortgage, RISA, UCC-9

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Rhode Island residents.

Right to Cure a Default in Rhode Island

In Rhode Island, borrowers facing default on a mortgage, vehicle loan, or retail installment contract may have statutory rights to cure - bring the account current and stop acceleration or repossession - before the creditor can complete foreclosure or sale.

This page covers four distinct cure regimes that apply in Rhode Island:

Mortgage cure / reinstatement under Rhode Island real property law.

Retail installment contract cure (vehicles, appliances, furniture).

UCC Article 9 default and cure for personal-property-secured loans.

Bankruptcy cure under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(5), which overrides state-law cure limits in Chapter 13.

Rhode Island Mortgage Reinstatement and Cure

RI uses non-judicial foreclosure (R.I. Gen. Laws Section 34-27-3.1). Reinstatement negotiable under deed terms.

Mortgage cure typically requires the borrower to pay:

All past-due principal and interest (arrearages).

Late fees and, where allowed, attorney fees and foreclosure costs.

Corporate advances (force-placed insurance, escrow advances).

Cure amounts must be detailed in a reinstatement quote. Under federal Regulation X (12 CFR Section 1024.36), a borrower can request this information in writing and must receive a response within 30 business days.

See mortgage cure rights for the full framework.

Rhode Island Retail Installment Cure

R.I. Gen. Laws Section 6-27-5 governs retail installment cure.

Retail installment contracts cover:

Motor vehicle purchases (most common).

Furniture and appliance purchases.

Cosmetic, dental, and elective medical financing.

Solar and home-improvement financed purchases.

Where Rhode Island law requires a cure notice, acceleration or repossession before that notice is issued (or before the cure window expires) creates a wrongful-repossession or UDAP claim. Damages can include the return of the collateral, statutory damages, and attorney fees.

R.I. Gen. Laws Title 6A Chapter 9 codifies UCC-9.

UCC Article 9 sets the default-and-disposition rules for personal-property-secured loans (vehicles, equipment, inventory). Under UCC 9-611 through 9-614:

The notice must give the debtor an opportunity to redeem the collateral (UCC 9-623) by paying the full balance (not just arrears) plus costs.
